picks.title: JARVIS: An Agent That Designs, Builds, and Tests Circuit Boards on Its Own
picks.abstract: Power electronics is central to the energy transition, but developing new hardware still relies on human-led design, fabrication, testing, and iteration. We present JARVIS, an embodied AI agent that autonomously closes this loop for circuit boards. JARVIS maintains machine-specific capabilities and constraints, scans its workspace using a robot-mounted 3D scanner, and constructs an executable digital twin in which it rehearses robot motions, fabrication steps, and circuit behavior before consuming materials. A single text instruction initiates the physical experiment. Using unmodified desktop equipment, the agent coordinates a robot arm, a PCB printer that deposits conductive silver ink and solder paste, and a pick-and-place machine. It verifies progress using cameras and sensors, then tests the fabricated circuit with an OPAL-RT real-time simulator and an oscilloscope. Based on the measurements, JARVIS diagnoses deviations from the design and generates a revised design in KiCad for subsequent rehearsal. In a demonstration involving a 60 Hz notch filter for grid-connected converter sensing, JARVIS completed a first-run experiment in 2 h 39 min without human intervention, achieving 50.6 dB attenuation at 60 Hz. Its digital-twin rehearsal identified five issues before fabrication, including a test criterion that would have incorrectly rejected a functioning board. During execution, the agent also resolved encountered faults autonomously. These results demonstrate an integrated agent-driven workflow for physical design, fabrication, measurement, and iterative improvement of power-electronic circuitry. To our knowledge, JARVIS is the first system in power electronics in which an agent closes the physical design-build-test-learn loop for circuit boards.

card.in_short: An embodied AI agent named JARVIS autonomously designs, prints, assembles, and tests physical circuit boards from a single text prompt.
card.picture_it: Like a robotic engineer in a workshop that takes a blueprint request, builds the gadget overnight, and tests it without human help.
card.key_term: Digital twin: a virtual replica of a physical system used to simulate and test behavior before real-world execution.
card.why_it_matters: Hardware prototyping could speed up dramatically, cutting development cycles for green energy and power electronics from weeks to hours.
card.future_signal: Autonomous AI systems are moving out of software chat boxes and into physical laboratories to run closed-loop material and hardware experiments.
card.ask: How does JARVIS handle unexpected physical anomalies, like a misaligned solder drop, that aren't captured by the digital twin?

picks.title: Born for the Task: Rethinking Quantum Chemistry with Foresighted Agentic Computing
picks.abstract: Quantum chemistry relies on general-purpose software, whose generality leaves many large-scale calculations beyond practical resource budgets. Coding agents make task-specific programs cheap to write, but not efficient ones easy to find: whether a computational strategy is accurate and fast enough becomes clear only after it actually runs at the target scale. We introduce MakoBORN, a foresighted agentic computing framework that synthesizes high performance quantum chemistry programs on demand. MakoBORN anticipates the behavior of each strategy before execution, extrapolating its error from representative small systems and predicting its runtime from the target-scale workload and measured hardware throughputs. Building on these predictions, MakoBORN unfolds the preset schemes of existing packages into independently configurable algorithmic components, selects the fastest strategy within the error tolerance from the predicted accuracy-runtime Pareto frontier, and guides coding agents to compile it with component-level performance predictions. For a Hartree-Fock calculation with 50,024 basis functions, MakoBORN finishes in 1.41 h on a single CPU node, 77$\times$ faster than the estimated runtime of a general-purpose baseline and still 9.8$\times$ faster with development time included. On a single GPU, MakoBORN completes the ubiquitin calculation in 2.1 h, the same order of runtime as the GPU-accelerated package Mako on 64 GPUs, and shortens the B-DNA duplex calculation from an estimated two months to 8.1 h (173$\times$).

card.in_short: MakoBORN is an agentic framework that predicts the performance and accuracy of quantum chemistry algorithms to generate hyper-optimized code on demand.
card.picture_it: Like an expert contractor who accurately calculates the fastest building method before laying a single brick, saving months of wasted labor.
card.key_term: Pareto frontier: the optimal set of choices where you cannot improve one metric, like speed, without sacrificing another, like accuracy.
card.why_it_matters: Drug discovery and material science simulations that previously took months can now run in hours, drastically lowering R&D costs for pharma and tech.
card.future_signal: AI agents are shifting from general-purpose assistants to specialized co-scientists that design bespoke computational tools for heavy science.
card.ask: How robust are MakoBORN's runtime predictions when moving to entirely new, untested hardware architectures?

picks.title: Keel: A Frontier Model Teaches a Vision-Language Model by Rewriting Its Weights
picks.abstract: Can a frontier model repair a vision-language model (VLM) by rewriting its weights? Small reasoning VLMs such as Qwen3.5 need such a repair: in thinking mode they fall into loops on many image questions, repeating themselves until the token limit, spending the whole budget and losing the answer. The usual remedies act on the decoding, leaving the looping model as it was, or must be told what to change. Yet the cause is written in the weights. Keel, the first agentic weight-editing method for VLMs on image tasks, finds and removes it there. Told only the symptom, an editor, a frontier multimodal LLM acting as an agent, locates the cause, edits the weights and tests them, with a failure census and instruments showing it the failing images and where the VLM attends; among several editors, the harness keeps only edits that clearly reduce the failure without lowering accuracy on questions no editor saw. The repair needs no training, keeps the model's size and per-token cost, and applies to already-edited weights. The editors expose where the loops live: from the original weights, independent editors on both models trace them to the attention outputs of the middle layers, and the smaller VLM stops consulting the image inside a loop. On Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-2B, across six image benchmarks from visual mathematics to GUI grounding, the edit removes most loops on every benchmark and shortens answers, and the edited models are significantly more accurate than the thinking models on average; the larger one gains most on GUI grounding, a task absent from the practice questions. Because the repair lives in the weights, it combines with budget forcing where held-out questions favor it: on the best available weights, Keel has the best average accuracy on both models, significantly above every training-free baseline we compare on the larger one.

card.in_short: Keel is a method that fixes persistent reasoning loops in small vision-language models by directly editing their internal weights instead of changing prompts.
card.picture_it: Like a mechanic opening up a car engine to adjust a stuck gear directly, rather than just putting a warning sticker on the dashboard.
card.key_term: Weight-editing: directly modifying the numerical parameters inside a neural network to change its behavior without retraining from scratch.
card.why_it_matters: Developers can fix specific model bugs and hallucinations instantly and cheaply, without expensive retraining or runtime latency penalties.
card.future_signal: Surgical, post-hoc editing of model weights is emerging as a practical alternative to massive reinforcement learning loops for fixing model flaws.
card.ask: How do you ensure that editing these middle-layer weights to fix a looping bug doesn't inadvertently break other nuanced visual capabilities?

picks.title: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction
picks.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a classical decoder fast enough to process syndrome measurements at the rate at which they are generated, and to return its decisions with low latency. This is most demanding for superconducting processors, whose fast syndrome cycles force a trade-off between decoding speed and accuracy. Decoders fast enough to keep up sacrifice accuracy, which must be compensated for with larger codes and thus additional physical qubits. Here we introduce Rapids, a streaming neural decoder that is both fast and accurate. We achieve this by co-designing the decoder with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA): the network is built from operations that map cheaply onto the device and trained in its integer arithmetic. For the distance-19 surface code, Rapids decodes each round of syndromes in under a microsecond on a single FPGA, fast enough for superconducting processors, and returns its decisions with the low latency that fault-tolerant algorithms require. Its logical error rate is 240 times lower than that of existing real-time hardware decoders. The same design extends to the color code and the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code, on which our decoder is 16 times more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder. We further show that the decoder scales: spread over several FPGAs or hardened into custom silicon, it becomes faster, more accurate, or able to decode larger codes. Classical hardware thus becomes a further resource, alongside qubits, that can be scaled to improve fault-tolerant quantum computers.

card.in_short: Rapids is a streaming neural decoder designed with FPGAs that processes quantum error correction fast enough and accurately enough for real-world computers.
card.picture_it: Like a lightning-fast traffic cop who spots and corrects highway lane errors instantly, preventing massive multi-car pileups.
card.key_term: Streaming neural decoder: an algorithm running on specialized hardware that detects and corrects errors in quantum data on the fly.
card.why_it_matters: It removes a major hardware bottleneck, making large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers commercially viable much sooner than expected.
card.future_signal: Co-designing AI models tightly with custom silicon like FPGAs is becoming essential for overcoming the physical limits of emerging computing paradigms.
card.ask: What limits how far this FPGA-based decoding architecture can scale as quantum processors grow to thousands of physical qubits?

picks.title: Beam Model Technical Report
picks.abstract: Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 501.3B total parameters and 23.4B active parameters, specifically built and optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. Beam delivers frontier level reasoning, while requiring 3-4x less inference compute than many models of its class. Pretrained on 23.8T diverse, curated, high-quality tokens, Beam features a 1M-token context window achieved through a novel two-stage midtraining phase, built on verifiable, correctness-anchored data. Post-training leveraged a large-scale, fully asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) campaign across 10.5K GB300 GPUs, generating over 100M rollouts over 4 weeks of training. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date. Across our evaluation suite, capabilities continued to improve as we increased RL compute, with no sign of a plateau. Supported by deep hardware-model co-design, FP8/NVFP4 quantization, and a 1.93B-parameter speculative decoding drafter (DFlash 2), Beam maximizes serving throughput with efficient, flexible deployment. Averaged across conversation turns and harm categories, Beam refuses or pivots on 88.9% of harmful requests while complying with 81.5% of harmless requests, achieving the highest refusal/pivot rate on harmful requests among open-weight models on the Pareto frontier.

card.in_short: Beam is a large Mixture-of-Experts model optimized for coding and reasoning, trained with massive reinforcement learning and hardware co-design.
card.picture_it: Like a high-performance sports car engineered so every single part is optimized for speed, using a fraction of the fuel of heavier trucks.
card.key_term: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE): an architecture where only a subset of a model's total parameters are activated for any given token, saving compute.
card.why_it_matters: Companies can deploy frontier-class coding and reasoning intelligence at a fraction of the usual inference cost.
card.future_signal: Scaling reinforcement learning for reasoning tasks continues to yield steady performance gains without hitting a plateau.
card.ask: How did you maintain model safety and high refusal rates on harmful prompts while aggressively scaling the reinforcement learning campaign for raw capability?

picks.title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
picks.abstract: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.

card.in_short: ROGUE-AI is a multi-agent auditing framework that replicates real-world AI security failures to prove that ordinary design oversights cause more harm than malicious attacks.
card.picture_it: Like a safety board recreating airplane accidents to discover that pilot confusion is a bigger hazard than sabotage.
card.key_term: Prompt injection: a security vulnerability where an attacker smuggles malicious instructions inside benign user input to hijack an LLM.
card.why_it_matters: Enterprise deployment teams must focus as much on guarding against simple environment oversights as they do on sophisticated hacker attacks.
card.future_signal: AI safety research is shifting from abstract jailbreak prevention to empirical, incident-based auditing of real-world operational hazards.
card.ask: Given that simple tool-output warnings successfully reduced harm, what is the best way to design these warnings so they don't annoy users or degrade agent productivity?

picks.title: MKA: Evaluating Multimodal Knowledge Agents on end-to-end professional tasks
picks.abstract: We introduce the Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark, which measures how well autonomous agents perform end-to-end professional knowledge work that depends on visual understanding. Each task requires an agent to extract and combine information from multiple visually dense files, such as CAD blueprints, electronics schematics, radiographs, complex charts and geospatial maps, and to produce a standalone deliverable in .xlsx, .pptx, .pdf, .docx, .html or .png format. Existing benchmarks leave this capability largely untested: removing image-viewing tools leaves Gemini 4 Carbon's score on GDPval unchanged, and single-format evaluations such as GDP$.$pdf and GDP$.$xlsx do not require reasoning across files or modalities. MKA contains 200 tasks across 10 economic sectors. Deliverables are graded against expert-weighted rubrics by a sandboxed agentic autorater that agrees with human domain experts on 96.2% of criterion judgments in our expert-graded study (Cohen's $κ= 0.91$), scored by weighted satisfaction rate (WSR) overall and on frontier criteria unsaturated by prior-generation models (Climb-WSR). Across the frontier models we evaluate (Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra), Claude Fable 5.2 (56.6% Climb-WSR, 73.3% Overall WSR) and Gemini 4 Carbon (54.3% Climb-WSR, 71.9% Overall WSR) achieve the highest scores, while Carbon uses $5.7\times$ fewer tokens. Even for the strongest models, Climb-WSR remains below 57%, leaving substantial headroom for multimodal agents.

card.in_short: MKA is a benchmark evaluating how well multimodal AI agents handle complex, cross-file professional knowledge work across various industries.
card.picture_it: Like a rigorous practical exam for a senior consultant, testing their ability to synthesize CAD blueprints, spreadsheets, and reports into one deliverable.
card.key_term: Multimodal knowledge agent: an AI system that can understand, reason across, and generate multiple types of data formats like text, images, and spreadsheets.
card.why_it_matters: It gives software buyers a reliable way to measure whether an AI can actually perform end-to-end white-collar work rather than just passing simple chat tests.
card.future_signal: AI evaluation is moving away from simple multiple-choice tests toward complex, multi-format professional simulations graded by automated expert rubrics.
card.ask: What are the main bottlenecks preventing top models from scoring above 60% on the harder criteria in this benchmark?
